claim: Proteins containing prion-like low complexity domains (PLDs) are common drivers of the formation of biomolecular condensates.
source: Proteins containing prion-like low complexity domains (PLDs) are common drivers of the formation of biomolecular condensates and are prone to misregulation due to amino acid mutations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about PLDs.

claim: Proteins containing prion-like low complexity domains are prone to misregulation due to amino acid mutations.

claim: The Mpipi residue-resolution coarse-grained model can quantify the impact of amino acid mutations on the stability of 140 PLD mutants from six proteins.
source: Here, we exploit the accuracy of our residue-resolution coarse-grained model, Mpipi, to quantify the impact of amino acid mutations on the stability of 140 PLD mutants from six proteins (hnRNPA1, TDP43, FUS, EWSR1, RBM14, and TIA1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulations performed in this study.

claim: Scaling laws exist that quantify the range of change in the critical solution temperature of PLDs as a function of the number and type of amino acid sequence mutations.
source: Our simulations reveal the existence of scaling laws that quantify the range of change in the critical solution temperature of PLDs as a function of the number and type of amino acid sequence mutations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations performed in this study.

claim: The scaling laws for PLD critical temperature changes are consistent with the physicochemical properties of the mutations.
source: These rules are consistent with the physicochemical properties of the mutations and extend across the entire family tested, suggesting that scaling laws can be used as tools to predict changes in the stability of PLD condensates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of simulation data.

claim: Scaling laws extend across the entire family of PLDs tested.

claim: Biomolecular condensates exhibit non-random molecular compositions.
source: Biomolecular condensates are highly multicomponent systems with remarkable specificity: they exhibit non-random molecular compositions and, concomitantly, contain distinct physicochemical environments defined by the collective behavior of their components (Banani et al., 2017; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase separation has emerged as a leading mechanism to account for the formation of biomolecular condensates.
source: Phase separation has emerged as a leading mechanism to account for the formation of biomolecular condensates.

claim: In phase separation, segregative (density-driven) and associative (connectivity-driven) transitions are coupled to produce protein- and nucleic acid-rich phases suspended in the cellular cytoplasm or nucleoplasm.

claim: Intrinsically disordered proteins/regions (IDP/IDRs) have emerged as strong contributors to the multivalency and phase separation capacity of many naturally occurring proteins.
